title: How to Use Class Discussions for TOK Essay Ideas
summary: Learn how TOK class discussions can produce focused essay ideas, knowledge questions, examples, counterclaims, and a practical fall-term plan.
body_markdown:
Class discussion is one of the best places to generate TOK essay ideas because it exposes disagreements, assumptions, examples, and alternative perspectives before you draft. The aim is not to record everything said. Instead, identify moments that reveal a **problem about knowledge** , then connect that problem to your prescribed title.


This approach is particularly useful during the **IB TOK fall term** , when many May-session students select titles and develop plans. A productive discussion can provide knowledge claims, counterclaims, examples, and qualified judgements.


### Start with the official TOK essay task


The TOK essay is not a free-choice philosophical essay. According to the[IB overview of Theory of Knowledge](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/theory-of-knowledge/) , students respond to **one of six prescribed titles** issued for their examination session, and the essay has a maximum length of **1,600 words** . It is externally assessed, so sustained focus on the title matters.


Class discussions should help you explore an official title, not replace it with your own topic. You may create a working knowledge question to clarify the underlying tension, but the submitted essay must answer the prescribed title exactly as issued.


Before a discussion, copy the title and identify:


- The **command phrase** , such as “to what extent”
- Central concepts such as evidence, values, interpretation, or reliability
- Any required **areas of knowledge** , or AOKs
- Words that allow more than one reasonable interpretation


The IB's[example TOK essay titles](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/theory-of-knowledge/example-essays/) illustrate how each title creates distinct conceptual boundaries.


### Listen for intellectual friction


Useful TOK ideas usually emerge when two reasonable positions conflict. An example that everyone finds interesting may still be weak if nobody disagrees about what it demonstrates.


Listen for:


- Competing interpretations of the same evidence
- Different standards of proof across AOKs
- Disagreement about source reliability
- Exceptions that weaken general claims
- Contrasts between producing, communicating, and acquiring knowledge
- Consequences that follow from accepting a claim


Suppose one student says photographs provide direct evidence, while another argues that framing, selection, and captions shape interpretation. The deeper issue is not merely that photographs can be biased. It is whether mediation necessarily reduces reliability or whether critical methods can compensate for it.


A working question might be: **Under what conditions can mediated evidence justify reliable knowledge?** This question is a planning tool, not a replacement title. RevisionDojo's guide to[turning TOK titles into knowledge questions](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/breaking-down-tok-essay-titles-what-are-knowledge-questions) explains this distinction further.


### Use a discussion capture sheet


Ordinary notes preserve information. TOK planning notes should preserve the structure of disagreement.


What was said? TOK concept Possible challenge Essay use


Scientific replication corrects unreliable results Reliability and method Replication can repeat methodological weaknesses Claim about self-correction


Historical accounts depend on archives Evidence and perspective Source comparison can reduce distortion Analysis of responsible interpretation


Mathematical proof produces certainty Justification Certainty depends on axioms and definitions Qualification of a broad claim


Audiences influence an artwork's meaning Interpretation Some readings remain poorly supported Evaluation in the arts


Record the original point during class, then complete the conceptual columns immediately afterwards. This preserves the exchange without distracting you from participating.


### Convert comments into essay components


A classroom comment becomes useful when it has a clear argumentative function.


### Extract the knowledge claim


Rewrite the comment as a general statement about knowledge. “The scientist changed the conclusion after receiving new data” could become: **In the natural sciences, reliability depends partly on openness to revision.** This moves from describing an event to examining how knowledge is validated.


### Identify the assumption


Ask what must be true for the claim to work. The statement above assumes that revision responds to stronger evidence rather than institutional pressure, commercial interests, or fashion. Testing assumptions helps you develop meaningful evaluation.


### Build a strong counterclaim


Avoid token opposition such as “Others may disagree.” A stronger challenge would be: **Revision can demonstrate responsiveness to evidence, but it can also reveal how unstable conclusions are when evidence remains incomplete.** RevisionDojo's[TOK counterclaim guidance](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-counterclaims-for-the-may-2026-tok-essay-titles) shows how counterclaims can directly test a position.


### Attach and verify an example


A classmate's reference is not automatically reliable evidence. Record names, dates, disciplines, and the exact dispute, then verify these details through credible sources.


Use examples as **test cases** , not decoration. Explain what the example demonstrates, analyse the relevant knowledge mechanism, consider a limitation, and connect the analysis back to the title. The guide to[linking examples with knowledge questions](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/the-art-of-linking-examples-to-knowledge-questions-in-tok-with-sentence-starters) provides useful sentence structures.


### Write a provisional judgement


Finish each note with “Therefore,” “This is convincing when,” or “This claim is limited because.” For example: **Therefore, revision strengthens scientific reliability when evidence and methods remain open to scrutiny, but revision alone cannot remove institutional bias.**


### Ask questions that produce usable ideas


Broad prompts produce broad answers. Ask questions that expose conditions, comparisons, and limitations:


- What must be true for this claim to hold?
- Would the reasoning work in another AOK?
- What counts as sufficient justification here?
- Is this example typical, exceptional, or disputed?
- Which perspective would reject this interpretation?
- Does the counterclaim overturn the claim or limit its scope?


Your teacher can clarify wording and help assess whether an example fits an AOK. However, the final interpretation, argument, and writing must remain your own.


### Build a September-to-November routine


The IB issues session-specific titles, but schools establish their own internal deadlines. Treat this schedule as practical advice and follow your coordinator's dates.


Period Discussion priority Output


September Compare titles and clarify terms Shortlist with one tension per title


Early October Test AOK combinations and examples Two possible AOK plans


Late October Develop claims and counterclaims One-page argument map


November Test the thesis and sequence Detailed outline or draft


After each lesson, spend **10 minutes** identifying the main disagreement, connecting it to a title, and writing a provisional judgement. Each week, remove ideas that cannot be verified or linked directly to the title. When selecting a title, look for a genuine dispute, contrasting AOK perspectives, precise examples, and a qualified answer. RevisionDojo's guide to[choosing a TOK essay title](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-tok-essay-title-that-works-for-you) offers a fuller checklist.


### Avoid common discussion-based mistakes


Do not treat the majority view as correct. Consensus may reflect shared assumptions or persuasive speaking rather than sound justification.


Do not copy another student's wording, thesis, or outline. The IB's[academic integrity policy](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/shared-resources/pdfs/academic-integrity-policy-en.pdf) requires authentic work and appropriate acknowledgement of sources.


Do not use unverified anecdotes or confuse frequent participation with structured planning. A strong paragraph still needs a claim, example, analysis, alternative perspective, evaluation, and link to the title. RevisionDojo's[TOK essay structure guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/structuring-for-success-in-ib-tok-essays) explains how to organise these components.


### Conclusion


Effective TOK discussion notes capture disagreements about evidence, methods, interpretation, authority, and justification. Convert those disagreements into claims and counterclaims, verify the examples, and finish with a judgement tied to the prescribed title.


RevisionDojo's TOK Resources and Jojo AI can help test knowledge questions and challenge counterclaims. TOK Study Notes and Coursework Review can then support planning and revision once your own argument is established.
